lesson.title: Sober Citizens, Sober Republic: The Rise of the Temperance Movement
lesson.summary: Alarmed by heavy drinking and its social costs, reformers energized by the Second Great Awakening built a temperance movement that pushed Americans toward moderation and eventually statewide prohibition laws.
lesson.body:
Americans in the early republic drank an enormous amount of alcohol by later standards, with hard cider, whiskey, and rum common at nearly every meal and social occasion. That habit came under sustained attack in the 1820s and 1830s as part of a broader wave of reform that grew out of the Second Great Awakening, the religious revival movement that swept the country beginning in the late eighteenth century and intensifying after 1800. Revivalist preachers taught that individuals could achieve moral perfection through their own effort and that a truly Christian society was within reach if enough people committed to reforming themselves and their neighbors, an optimistic, activist theology that fed directly into temperance, abolitionism, and other reform causes of the period.

Organized temperance work took institutional form with the founding of the American Temperance Society in Boston in 1826. The Society and the many state and local groups that followed it argued that alcohol abuse lay behind a wide range of social problems: domestic violence, poverty, workplace injuries in the new factories spreading across the Northeast, and the breakdown of family life. Early temperance advocates generally urged moderation rather than complete abstinence, but by the 1830s many organizations had shifted toward demanding total abstinence from distilled spirits and eventually from all alcoholic drink.

The movement built a substantial following through pledges, public meetings, and printed tracts, and it drew heavily on the same organizational tools abolitionists were using at the same moment: traveling lecturers, local auxiliary societies, and mass petition campaigns aimed at state legislatures. Temperance reform also gave many women, who could not vote or hold office, an accepted public role as moral guardians of the home and community, since drunkenness was widely blamed for the abuse and neglect wives and children suffered at the hands of drinking husbands and fathers.

That organizing paid off in law. In 1851 Maine passed the nation's first statewide prohibition law, banning the manufacture and sale of alcoholic beverages except for medicinal, mechanical, or industrial purposes, and within a few years more than a dozen other states had followed with similar so called Maine Laws. Many of these laws were later repealed, weakened, or struck down by courts, and prohibition would remain a contested, cyclical cause for the rest of the century rather than a settled achievement.

The temperance movement mattered beyond the fate of any single law. It showed how the revivalist energy of the Second Great Awakening translated directly into political organizing, and it helped build networks of reform minded activists, many of them women, who would carry the skills and convictions developed fighting alcohol into the fights against slavery and, later, for women's own political rights.
